title: Explaining the NFL’s commissioner’s exempt list: How does it work? Who is on it?
content:
Three players will start the 2026 NFL season on the commissioner’s exempt list, a designation primarily used in cases with pending disciplinary action.

The commissioner’s exempt list is a status assigned by commissioner Roger Goodell that prohibits a player from practicing, playing or attending games; however, upon request and with club permission, the player may be present at the team facility for meetings, individual workouts and non-football activities, per the NFL’s personal conduct policy. A player on the exempt list is paid his full salary, but he does not count against the team’s 53-man active roster. Essentially, the exempt list is like paid leave.

The personal conduct policy lists three circumstances in which a player may be placed on the exempt list:

1. When a player is formally charged with a felony or a crime of violence;

2. When an investigation leads the commissioner to believe a player may have violated the personal conduct policy;

3. When a violation relating to a crime of violence is alleged but further investigation is required.

The commissioner has sole power to place players on the list and remove them. Players may spend any amount of time on the list, per the commissioner’s decisions.

The personal conduct policy states that a player can appeal the designation to the exempt list within three days of being notified. The player would remain on the exempt list while the appeal is processed.

As detailed in the Collective Bargaining Agreement, players on the exempt list will be credited for the regular and postseason games missed against any suspension ultimately imposed.

• Green Bay Packers RB Josh Jacobs: Charged with misdemeanor battery and misdemeanor criminal damage to property from an alleged altercation at his home on May 23.

• Denver Broncos LB Jonathon Cooper: Facing charges of second-degree assault by strangulation, third-degree assault by knowingly or recklessly causing injury, criminal mischief, violating a protective order and harassment stemming from two June arrests over alleged domestic violence incidents. Cooper pleaded not guilty to all five charges on Monday.

• Seattle Seahawks CB Terrion Arnold: Facing kidnapping and armed robbery charges stemming from a February incident in Tampa, Fla.
